title: intermittent-edge-ttl-oscillation-incident-review
content:
Summary:

Short: On 2025-02-09 22:10 UTC we observed several ten-minute windows of elevated 5xx rates in EU-west across the edge fleet. Symptoms coincided with rapid, repeated DNS TTL changes from a provider pop, causing oscillating client egress paths and amplified cold KV-cache miss rates. Traffic shifts between legacy and warm-standby regions amplified token-level latency and triggered request timeouts for a subset of long-tail customer sessions.

Impact (approx):
- 14% of EU-west user requests experienced >1.5s tail latency spikes during windows
- 3% request error rate spike (5xx) for 12 mins total spread across three windows
- Affected customers: multiple mid-market tenants using dedicated EU regions; a handful of hosted API customers saw increased latencies

What happened (timeline, UTC):
- 22:07 first anomalous alert: small cluster of 5xx from edge-pop-eu1 (alert SRE-7983)
- 22:10 rapid DNS updates observed for edge-pop-eu1 from provider side (TTL changes from 300 -> 10s -> 300s over ~6m)
- 22:11 traffic steering controller recorded multiple rebalances: weighted-egress adjustments + automatic prefailover kicks
- 22:12 KV-cache miss rate increased by ~9x for affected routes (cold keys were primed slowly)
- 22:15 first manual mitigation: rate-limited traffic shift away from edge-pop-eu1 to eu-warm-standby (partial, 25% slice)
- 22:18 observed reduction in immediate 5xx but tail latency still high due to cold cache and increased upstream load
- 22:22 full 70% diversion to warm-standby, emergency cross-region burst enabled
- 22:28 stabilized baseline but notice of small error tail in long-running streaming responses
- 22:40 rollback of aggressive 70% diversion to limit cross-region egress costs; retained 35% slice for 40m while caches warmed

Immediate mitigation actions taken:
- Manual weighted egress shift using routing-controller: set egress weight for edge-pop-eu1 -> 30%, warm-standby-eu -> 70% (then adjusted)
- Enabled prefix KV pre-seed for top-1000 prefixes for critical customer routes
- Raised per-route token timeout for chat streaming endpoints from 45s -> 60s as temporary tolerance for cold start tails
- Put rate-limits on retries at the API gateway to reduce duplicate load during oscillations

Root cause hypothesis:
- Primary contributor: DNS provider intermittently propagated aggressive TTL oscillations for edge-pop-eu1 causing clients and intermediate resolvers to flip cached records quickly. That produced micro-second-level re-routing which the serving runtime and KV cache were not optimized to absorb in short windows.
- Secondary: our current weighted-shift automation conservatively treats quick DNS flaps as capacity signals and performed multiple small rebalances rather than a single stable diversion, causing thrash.
- Tertiary: absence of pre-seeded KV-cache for warm-standby region for many customer prefixes meant early-diversion traffic experienced cold-start overhead.

Why this is different from prior incidents:
- Not a pure zone outage — infrastructure nodes were healthy; instability originated at the DNS propagation layer and was amplified by routing loop behavior across caches/resolvers.
- Previous docs focus on steady failover; here the problem is oscillation (multiple short windows) and the interaction with client resolver TTL behavior.

What worked:
- Manual weighted-slice diversion was effective when held steady; once we stopped rapid rebalances latencies fell.
- KV pre-seeding for hot prefixes lowered misses on subsequent windows.
- Temporarily increasing streaming timeouts prevented customer-visible disconnects for some sessions.

What didn't work / surprises:
- Automation: our routing-controller has a cooldown of 30s which is too short for DNS TTL oscillation patterns; it ended up making multiple adjustments in reaction to resolver-level noise.
- Observability: our dashboards showed error spikes but lacked a quick cross-correlation view between DNS TTL changes (provider metrics) and kvcache-miss signals — engineering had to stitch logs.
- Cost controls: cross-region burst caused unexpected egress cost alerts; finance/ops were paged.

Immediate follow-ups (owners & deadlines):
- SRE: increase routing-controller cooldown window from 30s -> 180s for DNS-derived signals (owner: Arjun Patel, target: 2025-02-18)
- Infra: implement a kvcache pre-seed job for warm-standby that runs when a slice diversion >25% is executed (owner: Lena Ortiz, target: 2025-02-21)
- Observability: add a dashboard panel that overlays provider DNS TTL events, resolver miss ratios, and kvcache miss rate (owner: Tom Becker, target: 2025-02-17)
- Automation: add hysteresis rule to treat rapid repetitive DNS TTL flips as a single event (owner: Riley Chan, target: 2025-02-25)
- Runbook: add a short checklist for 'DNS TTL oscillation' incidents including safe diversion thresholds, pre-seed checklist, and an egress-cost kill-switch (owner: Maya Thompson, target: 2025-02-20)

Proposed runbook additions (draft bullets):
- Detection:
  - Alert: spike in regional 5xx + concurrent kvcache miss ratio >5x baseline + provider TTL variance >50% in 5m window
- Immediate steps:
  - Pause automated rebalancing (routing-controller pause)
  - Divert a conservative steady slice (start 30% -> hold 15m)
  - Trigger pre-seed for top N prefixes (configurable N; default 1000)
  - Notify finance ops if cross-region egress > configured threshold
- Escalation:
  - If steady diversion fails to reduce 5xx within 10m, escalate to oncall-sre L2 and consider full regional failover

Unresolved/questions for follow-up:
- Can we get TTL change events from provider as a feed? (we only pulled logs manually this incident)
- Is 30% the right initial diversion slice for all customers or should we prefer customer-tier-aware slices?
- Should routing-controller treat DNS-provider signals as lower-confidence than healthcheck-based signals?

Notes to self / raw ops commands used during incident (for runbook reproduction):
- routing-controller set-weight --region edge-pop-eu1 --weight 30 --reason "TTL-oscillation-mitigation"
- routing-controller pause-automation --reason "manual-hold-during-oscillation"
- kvcache-tool preseed --region eu-warm-standby --prefix-file top-1000-prefixes.txt --async
- api-gateway set-route-retry-policy --route /v1/chat --max-retries 1 --backoff-millis 500

Postmortem severity assessment: S2 (regional customer-impacting, no data loss, transient)

Communications:
- Customer notifications: short status email sent at 2025-02-10 00:05 UTC to impacted tenants; follow-up notice planned after runbook changes are implemented.
- Internal: incident IRC thread archived in Slack, post-incident blameless review scheduled 2025-02-19 15:00 UTC

Lessons and longer-term mitigations (notes):
- Add DNS-provider observability (tracer for TTL changes) into platform signals so routing decisions can be weighted appropriately.
- Pre-warm warm-standby caches for critical customers on any diversion action above a small threshold.
- Consider regional egress budget enforcement hooks to avoid uncontrolled cost spikes during emergency shifts.

Appendix / raw metrics links:
- kvcache-miss-rate timeseries: https://metrics.redwood.ai/d/kvcache/eu-miss?from=2025-02-09T21:50:00Z&to=2025-02-09T22:50:00Z
- routing controller audit: https://logs.redwood.ai/q/routing-audit?query=incident%20SRE-7983
- DNS provider feed (manual export): https://providerlogs.example.net/edge-eu1/2025-02-09-export.csv

Action tickets created:
- JIRA SRE-7991: routing-controller hysteresis for provider-signals
- JIRA SRE-7992: kvcache preseed job for warm-standby
- JIRA OBS-402: DNS-TTL-panel in SRE dashboard

Final note: keep this doc as a living runbook draft until the follow-ups land. This incident shows how external control-plane (DNS) noise can create internal thrash; prioritize signal quality over speed in controller heuristics.
